title: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941)
hook: in Auschwitz a Franciscan priest offers to die in place of a father of a family

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse of Lisieux, the Little Flower, and her little way. Your line was the little way. Today's story is heavy. Go gently.

Before the war, he was a busy man: a Polish Franciscan friar with round glasses and a head full of plans. He founded a friary near Warsaw that kept growing, ran printing presses, put out magazines, even started a radio station. He traveled to Japan and set up a friary there too. Then, in 1939, Germany invaded Poland. The friary sheltered refugees, Jews among them. In 1941 he was arrested, and that May he was sent to Auschwitz, where he became a number, 16670.

First, where we are. Auschwitz was the largest of the Nazi death camps. More than a million people were murdered there, and the great majority were Jews, killed because they were Jews. Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners and others died there too. Kolbe was one prisoner among very many, and his story sits inside that much larger grief. In the summer of 1941, a man escaped from Kolbe's block. As punishment, the camp's deputy commander lined the prisoners up and picked ten men to die by starvation in an underground cell. One of them, a Polish sergeant named Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and his children. Then Kolbe stepped out of the line. He said he was a Catholic priest, and asked to take that man's place. Nobody knows exactly why the officer agreed, but he did. In the starvation cell, survivors said later, Kolbe led the men in prayers and hymns, and the cell was strangely calm. After two weeks, four were still alive, Kolbe among them. On the fourteenth of August, 1941, they were killed with an injection. Gajowniczek survived the war. He lived into his nineties, and he was in Saint Peter's Square in 1982 when Pope John Paul the Second declared Kolbe a saint and a martyr of charity. Catholics hear in this the words of Jesus in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Kolbe hadn't known the man.
screen: `MORE THAN A MILLION MURDERED.` · `TEN MEN CHOSEN TO STARVE.` · `A PRIEST STEPS OUT OF LINE.` · `THE MAN HE SAVED LIVED.` · then, large: `GREATER LOVE THAN THIS NO MAN HATH.`

segments.voice: This isn't for feeling anything in particular; it's for remembering the millions murdered in the Holocaust, most of them Jews, whole families, whole towns. Then think of one, a child, a grandmother, a name you may have read, and hold that one person for a while. If you pray, you can pray for the dead; if you don't, keep a silence for them.
Maximilian Kolbe. A Franciscan priest who, in Auschwitz, gave his life in place of a stranger with a family.
Your line: he stepped forward. One step out of a line, for a stranger. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep St. Maximilian Kolbe's feast on August 14, the day he died; he is honored as a patron of prisoners and families, and pilgrims pray at the cell in Auschwitz's Block 11 where he died.

what a scholar hears: beatified in 1971 as a confessor, then canonized in 1982 as a martyr of charity, a category John Paul the Second chose for him.

notes: Douay-Rheims John 15:13 given from memory; confirm.

Auschwitz death toll: about 1.1 million, about 1 million of them Jews (Auschwitz-Birkenau Museum figures). The script says 'more than a million' and 'the great majority were Jews'. Confirm. The script deliberately places Kolbe's story inside the Holocaust of the Jews so it is not told as a Catholic story alone; a Keeper and a Jewish reader should check the balance.

Prisoner number 16670; arrival May 1941; escape and selection late July 1941; death by phenol (carbolic acid) injection August 14, 1941. Confirm details and whether naming the deputy commander (Karl Fritzsch) is wanted; the script leaves him unnamed.
Kolbe's friary Niepokalanów sheltered refugees, including Jews, in 1939–1940: commonly reported; confirm.
Kolbe's age: born January 8, 1894, so 47 in July 1941. Gajowniczek died 1995, aged 93.

Some historians have pointed to antisemitic content in prewar publications associated with Kolbe's presses; this is debated and is not in the script. A Keeper should decide whether the lesson should acknowledge it.
Practice: remembrance of Holocaust victims, phrased as an invitation; prayer for the dead offered 'if you pray'.
